alcoves.title: The Alcove of Firsts
alcoves.prompt: How do people decide who did something first?
alcoves.notObject: The plinth stays cold. A person, an essay or a summary is not an object you can stand in an alcove. Choose a thing: a record, a tool or a made object.

symbols.name: A pair of glasses (for 'perspective')
symbols.mirage: A shimmer rises from the plinth: the Symbol Mirage. Glasses can stand for 'perspective', but these glasses show no knowledge in the world. Nobody made, used or argued about them. The lamps stay dark. Choose a real, specific object.

symbols.name: A trophy (for 'being first')
symbols.mirage: The Symbol Mirage shimmers. A trophy stands for winning, but it shows nothing about how anyone decided who was first. The lamps stay dark.

symbols.name: A light bulb (for 'a new idea')
symbols.mirage: The Symbol Mirage shimmers. A light bulb is a picture of an idea, not a record of one. The lamps stay dark.

symbols.name: A crown (for 'who gets credit')
symbols.mirage: The Symbol Mirage shimmers. A crown stands for power, but this one shows no real decision about credit. The lamps stay dark.

objects.lit: The lamps glow. A patent is a real record, with a date, a number and an office that wrote it.

links.text: Loud's patent shows that, in 1888, a government office decided who could claim the idea, and wrote it down with a date.
links.response: The lamps burn steady. That is knowledge in the world: something real that people made, used or decided.

links.text: This patent shows evidence, perspective, power and culture.
links.response: A small stone golem walks up and ticks four boxes on its chest: evidence, perspective, power, culture. Then the ticks fall off, one by one. Naming concepts is not using them. Which ONE idea does this object change, and how?

links.text: This patent is old and interesting.
links.response: The lamps flicker and dim. Many things are old and interesting. What knowledge does THIS patent show in the world?

implications.text: So whoever keeps the records can shape who is remembered. In any field, I should ask who kept the records.
implications.response: The So-What Sphinx bows its stone head and steps aside. The alcove card fills with your words.
The So-What Sphinx does not move. 'Important to whom? What follows from it, here or somewhere else?'

implications.text: So a 'first' on paper can be different from a 'first' in use. A museum label should say which kind of first it means.
implications.response: The So-What Sphinx bows its stone head and steps aside. The alcove card fills with your words.

objects.lit: The lamps glow. A pen made between 1945 and 1948: a real thing that people used.

links.text: This pen shows evidence, perspective, power and culture.
links.response: A small stone golem walks up and ticks four boxes on its chest: evidence, perspective, power, culture. Then the ticks fall off, one by one. Naming concepts is not using them. Which ONE idea does this object change, and how?

links.text: This pen is old and interesting.
links.response: The lamps flicker and dim. Many things are old and interesting. What knowledge does THIS pen show in the world?

links.text: This pen shows that the design was made to work well enough to sell and use, not only to describe on paper.
links.response: The lamps burn steady. That is knowledge in the world: something real that people made, used or decided.

implications.response: The So-What Sphinx does not move. 'Important to whom? What follows from it, here or somewhere else?'

implications.text: So being first to make a thing work can matter more to its users than being first to have the idea.
implications.response: The So-What Sphinx bows its stone head and steps aside. The alcove card fills with your words.

implications.text: So an invention can be shared work, and credit to one famous name can hide the partners.
implications.response: The So-What Sphinx bows its stone head and steps aside. The alcove card fills with your words.

objects.lit: The lamps glow, but softly. This is a modern model, built from Loud's drawing.

links.text: This model is old and interesting.
links.response: The lamps flicker and dim. Many things are old and interesting. What knowledge does THIS model show in the world?

links.text: The workshop model shows what Loud's drawing can do when someone builds it today. It shows the design, not Loud's own pen.
links.response: The lamps burn steady. That is knowledge in the world: something real that people made, used or decided.

links.text: This model shows evidence, perspective, power and culture.
links.response: A small stone golem walks up and ticks four boxes on its chest: evidence, perspective, power, culture. Then the ticks fall off, one by one. Naming concepts is not using them. Which ONE idea does this object change, and how?

implications.text: So a reconstruction is evidence about a design, not about the past object. A label must say which it is.
implications.response: The So-What Sphinx bows its stone head and steps aside. The alcove card fills with your words.

implications.text: So a model can test whether an idea works, but it cannot tell us who used it first.
implications.response: The So-What Sphinx bows its stone head and steps aside. The alcove card fills with your words.
The So-What Sphinx does not move. 'Important to whom? What follows from it, here or somewhere else?'

objects.lit: The lamps glow. Ten real steel ingots, recorded by a museum.

links.text: The ten ingots show that crucible steel was traded as a raw material, before anyone made a blade from it.
links.response: The lamps burn steady. That is knowledge in the world: something real that people made, used or decided.

links.text: This set of ingots shows evidence, perspective, power and culture.
links.response: A small stone golem walks up and ticks four boxes on its chest: evidence, perspective, power, culture. Then the ticks fall off, one by one. Naming concepts is not using them. Which ONE idea does this object change, and how?

links.text: This set of ingots is old and interesting.
links.response: The lamps flicker and dim. Many things are old and interesting. What knowledge does THIS set of ingots show in the world?

implications.text: So a museum catalogue is evidence too, and it makes its own choices about names.
implications.response: The So-What Sphinx bows its stone head and steps aside. The alcove card fills with your words.
The So-What Sphinx does not move. 'Important to whom? What follows from it, here or somewhere else?'

implications.text: So the word 'Damascus' may name a market, not the place where the steel was made.
implications.response: The So-What Sphinx bows its stone head and steps aside. The alcove card fills with your words.

missions.title: The Alcove of Firsts
missions.knowledgeQuestion: How do people decide who did something first?

objectives.title: Optional: stand a real, specific object in the Alcove of Firsts (Hall of Firsts).
Optional: say what knowledge your object shows in the world.
Optional: answer the So-What Sphinx: what follows?

hints.text: A symbol stands for an idea. An object shows where knowledge happens.
Glasses for 'perspective' are a symbol, not an exhibit.
Use the Alcove of Firsts and choose one of your evidence cards that is a real thing.
Use the alcove next to the Hall of Firsts sign and choose 'Loud's patent, 1888' or 'Biro pen, 1945–1948'.
Say what THIS object shows, not what concepts it touches.
A list of concept names is not an argument.
Choose the sentence that says what people made, used or decided.
Choose the sentence that names a date, a use or a decision. Not the list of concepts, and not 'old and interesting'.
Choose a sentence that says what should change, here or in another field.
Choose a sentence that starts with 'So' and names a change. Not 'So ... is important'.

journal.text: The Alcove of Firsts: a symbol stands for an idea, but an object shows where knowledge happens in the world. Naming concepts is not using them. And every answer needs a 'so what?'.

awards.name: Lamp-Lighter
awards.earnedBy: You lit the Alcove of Firsts with a real object, said what it shows, and answered the So-What Sphinx.
